newsitem.title: USA: Unions' aid to Teamsters shows strike's high stakes.
newsitem.headline: Unions' aid to Teamsters shows strike's high stakes.

text.p: It isn't every strike that prompts the entire American labor movement to cough up millions of dollars for its brothers and sisters on the picket line.
But the International Brotherhood of Teamsters is not just any union, its strike against United Parcel Service is not just any struggle and union President Ron Carey is not just any labor leader.

It is the unique combination of these factors, labor experts say, that has prompted the AFL-CIO to recognize the high stakes involved in the UPS strike and to pass the hat among its 78 affiliated unions so that the strikers will continue to receive their meager $55 weekly picket line pay.
"This is the first time we've had such a major deal like this," said Ray Hilgert, professor of management and industrial relations at Washington University in St. Louis.

"This is such a high-visiblity, high-stakes confrontation, at least from labor's standpoint," said Hilgert. "This sort of posturing from the labor movement shows the company that labor is behind the Teamsters."

With the giant Teamsters union's treasury nearly depleted, AFL-CIO President John Sweeney announced on Tuesday that other unions in the labor federation will provide loans to cover the $10 million in weekly strike pay for the 185,000 UPS strikers "for a long strike, if that's what it takes."

While there is a long tradition of unions helping unions during bitter struggles, the potential magnitude of the bailout package -- if the strike lasts a year it could reach a half-billion dollars -- and the public flare with which it was done are rare, if not unprecedented, labor scholars said.

"The fact that it is on the front page and that Sweeney wanted it to be on the front page is crucial," said Michael Kazin, a labor historian at American University in Washington. "This is an attempt to show that they back up their people."
The show of solidarity has only a few parallels in history and probably none as large in cash terms, said labor historian Robert Zieger of the University of Florida in Gainsville.

They include AFL-CIO support for a farmworkers' strike and organizing drive in the 1970s and the bankrolling by the United Mine Workers of massive organizing drives in the steel and auto industries amid the founding of the Congress of Industrial Organizations in the 1930s, he said. The CIO and the American Federation of Labor merged in 1955 to form the AFL-CIO.

What prompted the 13.1 million-member AFL-CIO to rescue the Teamsters in this case was the widespread publicity the 10-day-old strike has received, the issues at the core of it and the fact it is the biggest walkout perhaps since the postal workers' strike of 1970, experts said.

A key union demand in the strike, that UPS convert some 10,000 of its lower-paid union workforce of about 110,000 into better paying full-time jobs, is an issue that reflects the thinking behind the "America Needs a Raise" theme that Sweeney has sounded since his election 22 months ago.

"I think the issues that the Teamsters are focusing on are clearly ones that the AFL-CIO is focusing on right now," said Michael Belzer a senior research associate at Cornell University's School of Industrial and Labor Relations.

If the show of solidarity produces at least a face-saving agreement, experts said, it will help support other organizing campaigns, including the Teamsters own efforts at recruiting members at the competitors of UPS, all of which are non-union.

Another reason for the AFL-CIO aid to its largest union is the close relationship between Sweeney and Carey, who was an early supporter of the AFL-CIO president's insurgency bid for the labor movement's highest office two years ago, they said.

When Carey narrowly defeated James Hoffa, son and namesake of the legendary Teamster leader, in December in an election that is still being investigated, Sweeney called it a "historic turning point for the labor movement" and hailed Carey as "a unique American hero."
Despite its image of wealth, power and previous corruption, the structure of the Teamsters, in which its 600 locals have a high degree of autonomy, has left the central union cash poor.
"The Teamsters are a very underfunded and poor union and always have been," said Belzer.

Adding to its woes was a decision at its 1991 convention to raise weekly strike pay to $200 without an accompanying mechanism to pay for it. The money the union had left in its war chest was depleted by a three-week national truck strike in 1994, for which it still owes other unions $10 million.
A source with knowledge of the union finances said other unions have the resources to come up with the aid package, even if the UPS strike lasts a year.
"There are some unions with pretty stubstantial treasuries," he said. "They can't do it painlessly but the resources are there if they put their minds to it."
